tasks.title: Projection: the columns you need
tasks.statement: Table customers(id, name, city). Output the name and city of all customers in ascending id order (columns: name, city).
tasks.hint: List the columns after SELECT and the table after FROM; ORDER BY sets the order.
tasks.starter:
-- name and city of all customers
SELECT

tasks.title: Selection: WHERE and ORDER BY
tasks.statement: Table products(id, title, category, price). Output the title and price of products costing more than 1000 rubles, the most expensive first (columns: title, price).
tasks.hint: WHERE price > 1000 ORDER BY price DESC.
tasks.starter:
-- products over 1000, by descending price
SELECT

tasks.title: Range and pattern
tasks.statement: Output the titles of products whose price is from 500 to 5000 inclusive and whose title contains the letter «f». Column title, ordered by ascending id.
tasks.hint: BETWEEN includes both bounds; `LIKE '%f%'` — the letter «f» anywhere. Note: in SQLite LIKE is case-insensitive only for Latin letters.
tasks.starter:
-- price from 500 to 5000 and the letter «f» in the title
SELECT

tasks.title: No duplicates
tasks.statement: Output the list of cities where customers live, without duplicates, in alphabetical order. Column city.
tasks.hint: SELECT DISTINCT city … ORDER BY city.
tasks.starter:
-- cities without duplicates
SELECT

tasks.title: Second most expensive item
tasks.statement: Output the title of the most expensive product excluding first place, that is, the second most expensive item (exactly one row, column title).
tasks.hint: ORDER BY price DESC, then LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1: skip one row and take the next.
tasks.starter:
-- second most expensive product
SELECT

tasks.title: No manager
tasks.statement: Table employees(id, name, dept, manager_id, bonus, salary). Who has no manager (manager_id is not set)? Output name.
tasks.hint: The comparison manager_id = NULL never fires: you need IS NULL.
tasks.starter:
-- employees without a manager
SELECT

tasks.title: COALESCE: gaps in bonuses
tasks.statement: Output the name and bonus of every employee, replacing a gap (NULL) in the bonus with zero. Columns: name, bonus; ordered by id.
tasks.hint: COALESCE(bonus, 0) returns the first value that is not NULL.
tasks.starter:
-- name and bonus (NULL → 0)
SELECT

tasks.title: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)
tasks.statement: In a single query output two columns: how many employees there are in total (total) and for how many a bonus is set (with_bonus).
tasks.hint: COUNT(*) counts all rows, while COUNT(bonus) skips NULL.
tasks.starter:
-- total and with_bonus
SELECT

tasks.title: NOT IN and NULL
tasks.statement: Table a holds the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and table b holds 2, NULL and 4. Output those x from a that are not in b (column x). A query with NOT IN will return nothing because of the NULL — find a correct one.
tasks.hint: NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery does not suffer from NULL in b; NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b WHERE y IS NOT NULL) also works.
tasks.starter:
-- x from a that are not in b (accounting for NULL in b)
SELECT

tasks.title: Constraints in a table
tasks.statement: Create a table accounts: id — an integer primary key; owner — text, required; balance — an integer, required, not less than zero (CHECK). The table must be named accounts, with the columns in this order.
tasks.hint: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner TEXT NOT NULL, balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0).

tasks.title: Foreign key
tasks.statement: Create a table invoices: id — a primary key, customer_id — an integer, required, referencing customers(id), amount — an integer. The columns must be in this order.
tasks.hint: customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) — a foreign key in the column definition.

tasks.title: Join: customer and order
tasks.statement: Output the customer name and order date for all paid orders (status = 'paid') in ascending date order, ties broken by name. Columns: name, created.
tasks.hint: orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id.
tasks.starter:
-- customer name and date of paid orders
SELECT

tasks.title: Three tables: what a customer bought
tasks.statement: Output the names of customers and the titles of products they bought in paid orders, without repeating customer–product pairs. Columns: name, title; ordered by name, then by title.
tasks.hint: The chain: customers → orders → order_items → products; DISTINCT removes repeated pairs.
tasks.starter:
-- customer and product in paid orders
SELECT

tasks.title: A join multiplies rows
tasks.statement: How many rows result if you join orders with order_items on order_id and filter nothing? Output a single number in the column n.
tasks.hint: Each order repeats as many times as it has items: COUNT(*) after the JOIN.
tasks.starter:
-- number of rows after joining orders and order_items
SELECT

tasks.title: Customers without orders
tasks.statement: Find the customers who have no orders at all, using LEFT JOIN. Output one column name.
tasks.hint: After LEFT JOIN, for customers without orders the orders columns are NULL: WHERE o.id IS NULL.
tasks.starter:
-- customers without orders
SELECT

tasks.title: LEFT JOIN: the condition in ON
tasks.statement: For each customer output the number of their paid orders (status = 'paid'), including customers who have none (then 0). Columns: name, paid; ordered by customer id. The condition on orders must go in ON, not in WHERE.
tasks.hint: COUNT(o.id) does not count NULL; the condition o.status = 'paid' in ON keeps customers without paid orders.
tasks.starter:
-- customers and the number of paid orders (including 0)
SELECT

tasks.title: HAVING: active customers
tasks.statement: Output the ids of customers who have at least two orders, and the number of orders (columns: customer_id, n).
tasks.hint: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2.
tasks.starter:
-- customers with two or more orders
SELECT

tasks.title: Revenue by category
tasks.statement: Compute revenue by product category — the sum of qty × price — for paid orders only. Columns: category, revenue; ordered by descending revenue.
tasks.hint: Join order_items, orders and products; WHERE o.status = 'paid'; GROUP BY p.category.
tasks.starter:
-- revenue by category (paid)
SELECT

tasks.title: Scalar subquery
tasks.statement: Output the titles of products whose price is above the average price of all products. Column title, ordered by id.
tasks.hint: The average price is a subquery in parentheses: price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products).
tasks.starter:
-- products above the average price
SELECT

tasks.title: EXISTS: there is a paid order
tasks.statement: Output the names of customers who have at least one paid order, using EXISTS. Column name, ordered by id.
tasks.hint: A correlated subquery: WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'.
tasks.starter:
-- customers with a paid order
SELECT

tasks.title: Collapse before joining
tasks.statement: For each paid order output the number of items (items = sum of qty) and the sum of payments (paid_sum). If you join both tables directly, the sums double: first collapse each branch separately (WITH or subqueries). Columns: id, items, paid_sum; only orders that have both items and payments; ordered by id.
tasks.hint: Each CTE gives one row per order; a JOIN of the collapsing queries no longer multiplies rows.
tasks.starter:
-- for paid orders: items and paid_sum without row multiplication
WITH

tasks.title: UPDATE … RETURNING
tasks.statement: Raise the price of all products in the category 'tech' by 10% (in whole rubles: price = price * 11 / 10) and return the changed rows: id and the new price (columns: id, price), in ascending id order.
tasks.hint: RETURNING id, price at the end of UPDATE returns the changed rows. Do not forget WHERE category = 'tech'.
tasks.starter:
-- raise tech prices by 10% and return id, price
UPDATE

tasks.title: UPSERT: ON CONFLICT
tasks.statement: Warehouse stock(id, qty). A delivery is arriving: 7 more units of product 2, and 4 units of product 3 (which is not in stock yet). With a single INSERT … ON CONFLICT perform both inserts so that the quantity grows for the existing product. The result is checked against the table.
tasks.hint: ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET qty = qty + excluded.qty; excluded is the row being inserted.
tasks.starter:
-- delivery: (2, 7) and (3, 4) via INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
INSERT INTO stock (id, qty) VALUES

tasks.title: Safe deletion
tasks.statement: Delete the cancelled orders (status = 'cancelled') together with their items: first the items, then the orders themselves. The result is checked by the row counts in orders and order_items.
tasks.hint: The order matters because of the foreign key: first order_items with a subquery on orders, then orders.
tasks.starter:
-- delete cancelled orders and their items
DELETE

tasks.statement: For each product output the title and a price tier: `expensive` for a price of 5000 or more, `average` from 1000 to 4999, otherwise `cheap`. Columns: title, tier; ordered by id.
tasks.hint: CASE WHEN … THEN … WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END; the branches are checked from top to bottom.
